records.name: Israel
records.summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

sources.summary: Haaretz: first-person account of a transgender traveller's ordeal at an Israeli airport — security insisting 'if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male', documenting gender-identity humiliation at border screening.
Jerusalem Post (2025 data): homophobic and transphobic violence rose in Israel during 2025 — official data showing an increase in anti-LGBTQ attacks.
Ynet: anti-LGBTQ violence hit a record high in Israel — dating-app traps and organised ambushes luring victims to attacks; record assault totals.
Haaretz: Trump's inflammatory rhetoric is affecting Israel's transgender community — US discourse spilling into local climate; trans Israelis report heightened fear.
Haaretz: Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing searches of transgender people — protocol change after complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees/travellers.
Jerusalem Post: registration of a person's previous name abolished for transgender people — document-change policy removing old-name traceability.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying page addressed trans rights in Israel - laws, protections and gaps.

Outright International (last update 12 Mar 2026): Israel at-a-glance — no criminalization of consensual same-sex acts in the criminal code, some legal protections, but no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register; baseline legal matrix.

records.name: Philippines
records.summary:
The Philippines is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), the SOGIE Equality Bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited

sources.summary: Outright/IGLHRC Philippines legal overview (fetched page): lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility updated 2023 to bar SOGI-based discrimination of clients; openly gay/bisexual people allowed in armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017 (uniform policy follows legal gender on birth certificate); Clerical Error Law RA 9048 (2001) blocks administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people (judicial order required) and the 2008 Supreme Court ruling in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan bars legal-gender change even after gender-affirming surgery.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): two killings in days — 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist/activist shot by an unidentified gunman inside a General Santos clinic the same day; Bahaghari says the cases are an urgent reminder to pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill, which has been stuck in Congress for 25 years — no national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Manila Bulletin report (May 2025) covers a foreigner arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas.

Interaksyon (10 Apr 2024): drag artist Taylor Sheesh (Taylor Swift impersonator) was physically struck on stage by a man from the crowd at Bayambang, Pangasinan's Kalutan Concert on 6 April 2024 — she called the attack traumatic and urged passage of the SOGIE Equality Bill; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Rolling Stone Philippines explainer (7 Feb 2025): 25 years of legislative inaction on the SOGIE Equality Bill; patchwork protections that do exist — SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur, Iloilo) and 32 cities/municipalities; Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (SOGIE harassment: P20k-40k fine and/or up to 1 year); Magna Carta of Women and Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic/homophobic/misogynistic slurs and ridicule (fines P1k-10k, up to 30 days, sensitivity seminar).

Rappler: trans Filipinos' legal gender recognition bill would let applicants — including minors with consent — choose markers beyond male/female (X/nonbinary), addressing the lack of a recognition process that drafter Chase Go says drives social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence; the Commission on Human Rights has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'; allies plan to endorse the bill to the 20th Congress (28 July).

WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel guide (2026 data as of 18 Jun 2026): Manila 'Generally Safe' — LGBTQ+ 69, but Trans travellers only 62 ('Exercise Caution'), HIV+ 81; same-sex relations never criminalised, deep gender-diversity traditions (bakla/tomboy), vibrant Pride/nightlife scene and high media visibility, but SOGIE Bill (filed since 2000) stuck, no marriage equality, Catholic Church resistance; accessibility caveat: 80% of Metro Manila's 46 train stations lack step-free entrances, only 5 of 46 LRT-1 stations have elevators.

HRW report (21 Jun 2017), 'Just Let Us Be': documents bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools, with law short on remedies at the time — basis-level evidence of school-setting climate for gender-diverse youth; includes Tagalog summary and recommendations.

records.name: Nigeria
records.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brut

sources.summary: BBC (Aug 2024): the beaten body of Abujan trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. For this record: a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

The Dial (Feb 2025): six months after Abuja Area Mama's killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. For this record: impunity is documented — police response to a trans victim's killing produced no arrests half a year on.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. For this record: current (2026) official foreign-office warning aimed squarely at LGBT+ visitors.

TimesLIVE (Mar 2025): a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; the SSMPA is described by those affected as a 'weaponised' law creating a climate of hostility. For this record: police extortion and violence against perceived-gay people, with the specific bribe amount and injury.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024), marking 10 years of the SSMPA: the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed. For this record: a decade-outcome assessment of the national criminalisation law, not just its text.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Apr 2024): 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians via Grindr and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; community counters with exposure forums (one admin's alert page drawing 43,000 followers) and sting operations. For this record: documented app-based luring crime specifically targeting queer people, relevant to a visitor using dating apps.

UK Home Office CPIN on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026): same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; Sharia law in all 12 northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. For this record: current official UK-government assessment of penalties, including the north/Sharia overlay.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Sept 2022) covers transgender Nigerians fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

records.name: Romania
records.summary:
Romania is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visito

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Oct 2024) covers the CJEU ruling that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights (the Mirzarafie-Ahi case on recognition of UK gender recognition).

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

records.name: Vietnam
records.summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 Civil Code (Article 37) was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented here. Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma and "red tape" in accessing care, and trans-competent providers are scarce.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, unrestricted bathroom access, and no criminalisation — but the stalled recognition means no practical gender-marker change on documents. This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and prac

sources.summary: DW (late Sept/Oct 2025): Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — HRW Asia director Patricia Gossman calls it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; Health Ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

Amnesty International Viet Nam 2025 report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague Penal Code arts 109/116/117/331 used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; Viet Nam re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council until 2028.

Lighthouse Vietnam study (Oct 2024): 'Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in Vietnam' - documents experiences and forms of SOGICE in the Vietnamese context, with comprehensive data needs analysis.

UN Viet Nam feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially northern-province and ethnic-minority trans women; framed as case for accessible legal recognition.

Saigoneer (June 2023): Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans Vietnamese describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

IRB Canada Response to Information Request VNM201080.E (30 Jun 2022): Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (Freedom House 3 Mar 2021); multi-source treatment briefing covering society/authorities in Hanoi and HCMC across education, employment, housing, health care.

Viet Nam News (Nov 2018): National Assembly expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per Outright (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

records.name: Uruguay
records.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected

sources.summary: Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI orgs registrable; intersex bodily-autonomy protections flagged incomplete. The current civil-rights baseline a trans visitor enters.

Full text of Law No. 19684 (26 Oct 2018), Uruguay's Comprehensive Law for Trans People: state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons -- the statutory backbone of the country's trans-protection regime.

Equaldex status grid for Montevideo (governed by national law): marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination, conversion-therapy ban and equal age of consent all legal/protected; hate-crime rules cover SOGI. Compiled status page, undated.
Presidencia release: the Executive promulgated the Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons (Ley 19684, Oct 2018) -- official confirmation the comprehensive trans-rights statute entered into force.
Freedom House Uruguay 2024: Free, 96/100 (political rights 40/40, civil liberties 56/60) -- strong general rights climate for trans visitors.

TDoR 2025 record: Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 Jul 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to 7 years for the murder -- documented lethal violence against a trans person with judicial follow-through.

la diaria (May 2024): trans health-service user Andreina Stuart denounced mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital (Maldonado); criminal complaint pending, hospital director pledged an administrative investigation after the judicial stage; local officials pressed for health-system updates.

Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material; Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.
